## In brief

Language models trained on natural protein or DNA sequences are widely used to predict whether a mutation is harmful. The idea is that a sequence the model finds likely is one evolution would allow. That assumption often breaks down: how likely a sequence looks also reflects which species happened to be sequenced and how they are related, not only what natural selection permits. The problem grows as models get bigger, which is one reason larger protein language models have stopped improving at this task.

We introduce Likelihood-Fitness Bridging (LFB). Instead of scoring a mutation in one sequence, LFB averages the model's score across related sequences that face similar selective pressures. Under a standard model of evolution this cancels out the effects of random genetic drift. LFB works with existing protein and genome language models, needs no retraining, and adds little computation.

Across large experimental datasets and clinical benchmarks, LFB consistently improves predictions for every model family and size we tested. It also reverses the performance plateau: with LFB, the largest protein language models become the most accurate.

## Key figure

::: {.key-figure}
![**Figure 1.** Likelihood-fitness bridging. The log-likelihood ratio of a substitution is a noisy estimate of its change in fitness. Placing the same substitution in related sequences that evolved under similar pressures gives several noisy estimates, and their average is a lower-variance estimate of the true effect. From Pugh et al., NeurIPS 2025.](figure1.png)
:::
